prime.problem: The previous card ends with dz, a push on every logit. Without a rule for carrying that push through y = x · W, no weight in the model can learn and nothing below the output head ever gets a gradient.
prime.fits: The second backward stop. It takes dz = (p − y)/3 from the softmax + cross-entropy card and turns it into dWout for the update and dh for the final LayerNorm. It reuses the matmul from card 2 and the chain rule from card 3.
expect: one entry as a sum over positions
prime.goal: Write the backward pass of any linear layer from its shapes alone, compute dWout[1,3] = −0.6103 and dh[2,0] = 0.2976 by hand, and explain why the gradients of a shared weight add.

attend: Where does Wout[1,3] appear in the forward pass, and how many times?
Why do the three positions' pushes on one weight add instead of being averaged, given that the loss is a mean?
dW sums over positions while dx sums over output columns. What decides which size disappears?
When W is square, why can't the shapes alone tell xᵀ · dy from dyᵀ · x?
If a weight matrix is all zeros, which gradients still flow and which are blocked?

must: z[t,j] = Σ_i h[t,i] · W[i,j] → W[1,3] appears in z[t,3] at every position, scaled by h[t,1] → chain rule adds one term per use → dWout[1,3] = Σ_t h[t,1] · dz[t,3] = −0.0193 − 0.0569 − 0.5340 = −0.6103
A gradient has the shape of its variable → dW must be in × out (4 × 5) → from x (3 × 4) and dy (3 × 5) only xᵀ · dy fits and comes out 4 × 5 → the shared size, T, is summed away
h[t,i] fed all 5 logits of its row through W[i,j] → dh[t,i] = Σ_j dz[t,j] · W[i,j] → dx = dy · Wᵀ, (3 × 5)(5 × 4) = 3 × 4 → dh[2,0] = 0.2976, and a zero W blocks every gradient below it

One weight is shared by every position → each position is a training example → their gradients add (the mean's 1/3 is already in dz) → the same rule, dW = xᵀ · dy, serves Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo, W1, W2 and Wout (all match PyTorch to ~1e-16)
elevated: PyTorch's nn.Linear stores W.T, shaped (out, in) → its weight.grad is dWᵀ (5 × 4 for the head, entry [3,1] = −0.6103) → load and compare with a transpose, as tiny.py's torch_check does
A bias is added to every row → its gradient is dy summed over rows → dc2 = df.sum(0) = [0.2764, 0.1680, 0.0066, −0.4510]
reference: Plain text: dW = x.T @ dy; dx = dy @ W.T; db = dy.sum(0)
Tiny model shapes: h 3 × 4, Wout 4 × 5, dz 3 × 5, dWout 4 × 5, dh 3 × 4
Nudge check: Wout[1,3] + 0.001 changes the loss by −0.000610, ratio −0.6102

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–5 sentences how the output head's gradient dWout and the passed-down gradient dh come out of dz, and why the shapes force the formulas. Or draw the three boxes hᵀ · dz = dWout with their sizes, and the three pushes that add up to dWout[1,3].
checklist: one entry first: dW[i,j] = Σ_t x[t,i] · dy[t,j], a sum over positions
dW has W's shape, in × out, so it must be xᵀ · dy
dx has x's shape, T × in, so it must be dy · Wᵀ
gradients add because one weight is used at every position
a bias gets dy summed over rows

retrieve.q: Explain to a friend why a weight's gradient is a sum over positions, using the idea that the same weight is reused.
answer: every position runs its own copy of x[t] · W with the same W
nudging W moves the output at every position at once
so the loss's slope is the sum of the slopes through each use
the mean's 1/3 is already inside dy, so there's no extra division

retrieve.q: Walk through computing dWout[1,3] and dh[2,0] from h, dz and Wout, naming which row or column each uses.
answer: dWout[1,3]: column 1 of h times column 3 of dz, summed over t
dh[2,0]: row 2 of dz times row 0 of Wout, summed over the 5 words

retrieve.q: A colleague writes a backward pass using only shape matching and gets the right shapes everywhere, but training goes wrong on the attention projections. What could the shapes have missed, and how do you catch it?
answer: Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo are square 4 × 4, and x and dy are both 3 × 4
dyᵀ · x is also 4 × 4 but is the transpose of the right answer
derive one entry by hand, or run a nudge test, or compare with autograd
shapes are necessary, not sufficient

compare.q: That card produced dz = (p − y)/3; this one consumes it. What does each rule depend on, and which one changes if you swap the loss for another?
answer: p − y depends on the softmax + cross-entropy pairing
dW = xᵀ · dy depends only on the layer being x · W
a different loss changes dz but not the linear-layer rule
together they give dWout = hᵀ (p − y)/3

compare.q: The 6-weight network had dL/dW1 = [[0, 0], [−0.696, −1.392]] for one input. How is that the same rule as here, and what changes when there are 3 positions?
answer: there it was one example: dW is an outer product of one input and one gradient
here each position gives its own outer product h[t]ᵀ · dz[t]
with 3 positions the 3 outer products add, which is xᵀ · dy
ReLU zeroed a row there; here nothing is zeroed but the sizes are uneven

compare.q: Attention has A · V and Q · Kᵀ, products with no weight in them. How does this card's shape logic carry over, and what is different?
answer: the same logic gives dA = dC · Vᵀ and dV = Aᵀ · dC
both factors are activations, so both get a gradient and both are passed down
Q · Kᵀ has a transpose in the forward pass, so dK picks up one too
after that, dWq = aᵀ · dQ is this card's rule again

predict.q: Suppose the tiny model saw a 6-token sequence instead of 3, with the loss still the mean over positions. What happens to the shapes of dWout and dh, and to how many terms each entry of dWout sums?
predict.answer: dWout stays 4 × 5, because it has Wout's shape, whatever the length. dh grows to 6 × 4, one row per position. Each entry of dWout now sums 6 terms, and dz carries 1/6 instead of 1/3, so the gradient doesn't grow just because the text got longer.

apply.done: You predicted and saw: dh all 0.0000, every gradient below the head 0 (PyTorch agrees to 2.5e-16), but dWout nonzero, with dWout[1,3] = −0.4945 from dz = (0.2 − y)/3.
apply.hint: dx = dy · Wᵀ needs W; dW = xᵀ · dy only needs the input.
